en: Preface by the Disciple Tanlin: The Great Master Bodhidharma, who briefly expounded the Fourfold Contemplation for Entering the Way according to the Mahāyāna, was a native of South India in the Western Regions. He was the third son of a Brahmin king.

He was a man of divine wisdom and clear intelligence; whatever he heard, he immediately understood. His resolve was set upon the path of the Mahāyāna, and thus he abandoned the white robes of lay life to follow the black robes of the monastic order.

He succeeded in upholding the holy lineage, with his mind settled in profound stillness. Possessing comprehensive insight, he was enlightened regarding both worldly affairs and the inner spiritual realm.

His virtue transcended the mundane world. Moved by compassion and regret that the true teaching had declined in the borderlands, he was able to travel far across mountains and seas to wander and transform beings through his teachings.
During the Han and Wei dynasties, there was no scholar who had lost his worldly mind who did not turn to it with faith; yet those who clung to their own views gave rise to ridicule and slander.
At that time, there were only these two śramaṇas, Daoyu and Huike; though young in years, their noble aspirations were lofty and far-reaching.
Fortunately, I encountered the Dharma Master and served him for several years. With reverent devotion, I diligently sought instruction and received the Master’s guidance.

Moved by my sincere earnestness, the Dharma Master taught me the True Way, instructing me to settle the mind in this manner, to initiate practice in this manner, to accord with things in this manner, and to employ skillful means in this manner.
These are the methods for settling the mind according to the Mahāyāna, ensuring that there is no error or deviation. Thus it is said:
"Peace of mind" refers to wall-contemplation. "Thus initiating practice" refers to the four practices. "Thus conforming to things" refers to guarding against censure and suspicion.
"Thus employing skillful means" refers to dispelling non-attachment. This is a brief account of the origins [of this teaching].
Now, there are many paths for entering the Way; to summarize them, they do not exceed two kinds: first, entry through principle (li-ru); second, entry through practice (xing-ru).

As for entry through principle, it means awakening to the fundamental source by relying on the teachings. One must have deep faith that all living beings share the same true nature, which is merely obscured by adventitious delusions and cannot manifest clearly.
If one abandons delusion to return to the truth, one should remain concentrated in the "wall-contemplation" (bi-guan), without...
There is no "other" apart from oneself; ordinary beings and sages are equal and one, firmly abiding without shifting.

No longer following the teachings of words and letters, this is to be in profound accord with principle (*li*), free from all discrimination. This state of stillness and non-action is called "entry into principle. As for "entry into practice," it refers to the four practices;
all other practices are entirely contained within these. What are the four? First, the practice of requiting grievances; second, the practice of following conditions; third...
The practice of seeking nothing. Fourth, the practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What is it? It is the practice of requiting grievances. This means that when a practitioner of the Way undergoes suffering, they should reflect to themselves:

"Throughout countless kalpas in the past, I abandoned the fundamental for the derivative and wandered through the various realms of existence, giving rise to many grudges and hatreds and committing infinite acts of harm and injury. Now..."
Although there is no transgression, this is the ripening of the fruit of my past calamities and evil karma;
it is not something that gods or humans can grant to me. I accept it with a willing heart, without any resentment or complaint. As the Sutra says: "Encountering suffering, one does not grieve.

Why is this? Because of thorough understanding. When this mind arises, it accords with principle; by taking offense as the body of practice, one advances on the Path. Therefore, it is called the Practice of Requiting Offenses.

Second, regarding those who act in accordance with conditions: sentient beings lack a self and are all driven by karma. They experience both suffering and pleasure equally, as everything arises from conditions.
If one obtains superior retributions such as honor and fame, these are merely the results induced by past causes;

now that they have been attained, when conditions are exhausted, they will vanish again. What cause for joy is there? Gain and loss follow conditions, and the mind neither increases nor decreases. This is the wind of joy.
Being immovable and in profound accord with the Way, one is therefore said to "act in accordance with conditions.

Third, regarding the practitioner who seeks nothing: worldly people are long deluded, greedily craving and clinging to things everywhere; this is called "seeking. The wise, having awakened to the True Principle, turn back from the mundane.
They settle their minds in non-action while their forms follow the turning of events. All phenomena are thus empty and have no [inherent] location.
Vows and desires, as well as merit and darkness, constantly follow one another. Dwelling long in the three realms is like being in a house on fire;

all who possess a body experience suffering—who could find peace? Having thoroughly understood this state, one abandons all forms of existence, ceases conceptualization, and seeks nothing more. As the Sūtra says:
All seeking is suffering; the absence of seeking is bliss. To discern that the pursuit of non-seeking constitutes the practice of the Way is why it is called "the practice of non-seeking.

Fourth, regarding the "practice in accordance with the Dharma": the principle of intrinsic purity is designated as the "Dharma. This principle is empty of all manifold characteristics and is without...
In defilement, there is neither attachment nor this, nor that. The Sūtra says: "The Dharma has no sentient beings, because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings;
the Dharma has no self, because it is free from the defilement of the self. If a wise person can believe and understand this principle, they should act in accordance with the Dharma.
The essence of the Dharma is free from stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth; one practices the giving of *dāna* with a mind devoid of regret or attachment.

Having realized the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa*), one does not rely upon or cling to them, acting solely to remove defilements. One transforms sentient beings according to their needs without grasping at signs.
This constitutes both self-cultivation and the benefiting of others, and it serves to adorn the path to Bodhi. As it is with *dāna*, so it is with the other five perfections. For...
To practice the six perfections while eliminating deluded thoughts and yet performing no action— this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma.
*The Fourfold Practice Contemplation of Master Daomō (End)* *Epitaph and Verses for Master Daomō (Appendix)*
Emperor Wu of Liang, Xiao Yan, sat atop Mount Laṅkā upon a precious sun. Within it was a golden man wearing coarse hemp robes;
his form was like the great earth, his body like space, his mind like lapis lazuli, and his color like snow.
Neither polished nor burnished, it is eternally pure and luminous; With clouds and mist dispelled, the mind is thoroughly penetrating.
Using the *puṇḍarīka* flower to adorn the body, One follows conditions with constant joy.
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither coming nor going, With much learning and eloquence, there is no dharma to be preached.
Truly real, yet empty; transcending birth and existence, Whether great or small, all conditions severed— In a single instant, one ascends to the mind of wondrous enlightenment.
Leaping scales in the ocean of wisdom, the primordial principle arises;
The water of the Dharma should flow forever long. How unexpected that after a moment’s surge, one is again thirsty!
The pearl from the black dragon has fallen into the inner lamp of the mind; the white tuft of wisdom-blade meets the edge of the spearhead.
On the path of birth, the bird-like wisdom-eye suddenly closes; the river of dhyāna halts its flow and the bridge of Dharma breaks.
Without going or coming, without right or wrong, the physical forms of self and other shatter into fragments.
Dwelling in the void, both "go" and "come" return to stillness; within that stillness, how could there ever be a trace of choked emotion?
To employ this is to grasp the hand and transmit the lamp; birth and death, coming and going, are like a flash of lightning.
If one can possess a sincere heart free from doubt, then even when the fires of the kalpa burn, this lamp shall not be extinguished.
The single true Dharma is fully present; for those who have not yet awakened, this is the exhaustion of the deluded path.
